items.title: Methodological Approaches to Solving Tasks of Occupational Health and Safety Forensic Examination
items.abstract: The article presents methodological approaches to conducting forensic examination of occupational health and safety which, in turn, are based on a systemic-activity approach and consist of a sequence of interrelated stages aimed at establishing the causes, circumstances, and consequences of accidents and incidents. The purpose of using them is to ensure the comprehensiveness, objectivity, and reproducibility of the expert examination, as well as its focus on preventing similar incidents in the future.

items.title: Mitochondrial capacity limits neuronal energetic feasibility under chronic behavioural stress associated with AI-intensive environments: a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter
items.abstract: Abstract Sustained cognitive engagement, short and mistimed sleep, chronic stress and reduced recovery co-occur in AI-intensive environments, yet how this profile acts on brain energy metabolism is unknown. We built a neuron–astrocyte genome-scale model of human grey matter from Human-GEM v2.1.1, contextualised each cell with human single-nucleus expression, made transport, sodium-pumping and glutathione-recycling costs explicit, and calibrated one parameter to measured cerebral glucose use. Without further fitting the model reproduced the astrocytic share of oxidative metabolism measured by ¹³C spectroscopy (15.7% vs 14%), both the oxidative and the glycolytic regimes of human brain activation, and an independent reconstruction; deletion of genes causing inherited brain-energy disorders compromised its energetic margin far more often than deletion of other genes (odds ratio 79, p = 6 × 10⁻²⁰). Translating the five stressors into constraints, sleep loss and cognitive load each exhausted the margin within the protocol range, at a 25% loss of mitochondrial capacity and a 39% rise in signalling demand, whereas circadian misalignment, chronic stress and reduced recovery acted on arms with reserve. Combined, the stressors exhausted the margin at 0.72 times the moderate profile; across 400 parameter draws demand was met in 99.2% at low and 28.5% at moderate exposure. Substrate oxidation, not substrate supply, set the margin: restoring sleep or reducing load restored it, whereas ketone bodies, lactate or fibre-derived acetate helped only when glucose delivery itself was limiting. Results held across thresholds, releases, solvers and enzyme-capacity limits, and the thresholds are testable with ³¹P and ¹³C spectroscopy.

items.title: Model Immunization Beyond Condition Numbers: The Importance of Plateau Regions
items.abstract: Harmful fine-tuning can rapidly compromise safety alignment in Large Language Models, underscoring the vulnerability of deployed models to post-release modification. While prior work motivates model immunization by inducing ill-conditioned curvature to slow harmful optimization, this approach is not scalable due to the high computational cost of Hessian estimation. We refine this paradigm by extending the theoretical framework to prioritize plateau regions alongside curvature. We further introduce an immunization algorithm based on efficient Hessian estimation and bounds on the extremal singular values of the Hessian. We demonstrate the proposed immunization framework in three applications: (i) Fine-tuning-as-a-service settings where benign user data may be mixed with poisoned harmful data, (ii) open-weight settings where an adversary can fine-tune on harmful-only data with varied training dynamics, and (iii) robust unlearning, where immunized models better resist relearning attacks after unlearning. Extensive experiments confirm that our approach achieves robust defense against adversarial fine-tuning while largely maintaining general utility and downstream trainability. Our code is available at https://github.com/minhquoc0712/BECON.

items.title: Multi-LLM Agentic AI at the Edge: Joint Agent Scheduling and Resource Allocation
items.abstract: In this paper, an edge-enabled multi-large language model (LLM) agentic AI architecture is proposed, where one supervisor AI agent and multiple worker AI agents cooperatively execute users' requests at the edge. The supervisor AI agent decouples the user request into a series of sub-tasks and dynamically dispatches them to LLM-equipped worker AI agents via two agentic workflows, i.e., parallel and serial workflows, with a two-level retry mechanism to enhance execution reliability. To prolong the service duration of worker AI agents, the energy minimization problems are formulated by jointly considering AI agent selection and resource allocation, subject to task execution latency and quality of service (QoS) constraints. A resource allocation scheme based on alternating optimization (AO) is proposed. Specifically, for the parallel workflow, the scheme decouples the original problem into bandwidth allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems, which are iteratively solved by the proposed successive convex approximation (SCA), Lagrangian relaxation (LR), and Gale-Shapley (GS) or LLM-based algorithms, respectively. For the serial workflow, the problem is similarly decoupled into service time allocation, retrieval selection and AI agent selection sub-problems; the optimal service time allocation is obtained via Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, while the latter two sub-problems are addressed by extending the proposed algorithms to the serial scenario. Simulation results show that the proposed resource allocation scheme can reduce system energy consumption compared with other benchmarks, while experiments on a multi-LLM agentic AI system based on Qwen and Llama demonstrate improved task execution success rates.

items.title: Multimodal evaluation of cognitive load during prosthetic device use in activities of daily living
items.abstract: The cognitive burden associated with upper-limb prosthesis use remains a barrier to functional adoption, yet existing evaluations often rely on single-modality measures. This study investigates a multimodal framework for assessing cognitive load during activities of daily living. Twelve participants without limb loss performed standardized activities of daily living using their natural hand and a simulated tendon-driven prosthesis in a within-subject design. This controlled baseline was used to evaluate modality-specific responses to prosthesis-mediated task demands across subjective, behavioral, and neurophysiological measures. Cognitive workload was assessed using task performance metrics, subjective ratings from the NASA Task Load Index (NASA-TLX), eye-tracking measures including gaze behavior and pupillary dynamics, and prefrontal cortical activation measured with functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Prosthesis use increased NASA-TLX mental demand by 2.80–3.85 points across tasks (all p < 0.001) and prefrontal oxygenated hemoglobin by 0.96–1.14 μ M across regions during carton transfer and pour (all p < 0.001). Pupillary activity differentiated conditions during block transfer ( p < 0.001) and checker transfer ( p < 0.05), but not carton transfer and pour ( p = 0.47), demonstrating task-dependent responses across modalities. A multimodal framework provides a more comprehensive assessment of cognitive load than any single measure alone, offering valuable insights into how cognitive demand manifests across behavioral, perceptual, and biological domains. This framework establishes a controlled baseline for multimodal cognitive workload assessment and provides a foundation for future investigations in individuals with limb loss.

items.title: Multimodal situation awareness for big data environments via adaptive sampling and dual self-distillation
items.abstract: Situation awareness (SA) in disaster management requires robust modeling of multimodal big data from complex environments. With the increasing availability of large-scale video and audio data from surveillance systems, drones, and public sensors, multimodal approaches have become essential for improving reliability. However, existing methods often rely on uniform data sampling and treat modalities equally, limiting their effectiveness when data quality varies across time and modality. Compared with our previous work, this study extends from modality-specific analysis to a multimodal audio–visual framework. To address these challenges, this paper proposes MSA-SD², a multimodal situation awareness framework specifically designed for big data environments based on selective dual self-distillation. An adaptive temporal sampling and alignment module is introduced to prioritize informative temporal segments and ensure consistent audio–visual correspondence, enabling efficient processing of large-scale multimodal big data. For visual representation, a superpixels-guided vision transformer is employed, while a transformer-based audio encoder models temporal acoustic patterns. A multimodal student model is guided by visual and audio teacher models through a selective distillation strategy that adapts to modality reliability. Experimental results demonstrate improved performance on large-scale multimodal datasets, particularly under challenging big data conditions with varying data quality across modalities.

items.title: NL2RCtrl: Risk-Controlled Controller Synthesis from Natural Language Requirements
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have enabled the translation of natural language (NL) requirements into linear temporal logic (LTL) specifications, facilitating controller synthesis for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, the reliability of such translations remains a concern in safety-critical applications, particularly when NL requirements are ambiguous. This paper proposes a framework based on Conformal Risk Control (CRC) to provide a statistical guarantee on the risk of issuing a controller that violates the user's intended requirement. Rather than requiring semantic equivalence between the generated and intended specifications, the proposed approach considers language inclusion, a sufficient condition for ensuring that the traces of a controller synthesized for the generated specification satisfy the intended requirement. To account for ambiguity, the LLM is queried multiple times, and the resulting LTL specifications are grouped into semantic equivalence classes and ranked by their frequency of occurrence. Given a prescribed risk level, CRC selects how many of the top-ranked equivalence classes to combine into a single LTL specification, such that the probability of issuing a controller that violates the intended requirement is bounded by that level. A controller is then synthesized for the resulting specification, or the framework abstains. Experiments on a vehicle navigation case study evaluate the proposed approach.

items.abstract: Human resource development in the modern era emphasizes not only professional knowledge and work performance but also workplace safety as a fundamental factor for organizational sustainability. This academic article aims to analyze the principles of human resource development based on workplace safety concepts, focusing on situation awareness and effective decision-making in reducing work-related risks and enhancing organizational development. The analysis indicates that personnel equipped with safety knowledge, situational awareness, and analytical skills are more capable of making appropriate decisions, minimizing human errors, and promoting life and workplace safety. Furthermore, recognizing people as the key mechanism of organizational development contributes to the establishment of a strong safety culture that supports work efficiency, collaboration, and sustainable organizational growth. Therefore, human resource development under workplace safety principles is essential.

items.title: Occupational dust and noise exposure and worker health in the non-ferrous metal mining and processing industry in Guangxi, China, 2021–2025
items.abstract: Background Occupational hazards remain a substantial concern in the non-ferrous metal mining and processing industry. Using Guangxi’s abundant non-ferrous mineral resources, this study analyzed workplace occupational-hazard monitoring and occupational health examination data to support evidence-based prevention and control of occupational diseases in the region. Methods Using data from the monitoring system for 2021–2025, we conducted descriptive analyses of workplace occupational hazards and applied multivariable logistic regression models to identify factors associated with workers’ abnormal pulmonary function and high-frequency hearing loss. Results Between 2021 and 2025, a total of 306 enterprises and 2,379 positions were monitored. Noise showed the highest cumulative exceedance rate (33.1%), followed by dust (11.7%; C TWA exceedance of 20.0% for silica dust versus 1.2% for other dust) and lead (1.3%). Over the five-year period, workers’ exposure rates to all hazardous agents declined consistently (all p for trend < 0.001), and the silica dust exceedance rate also decreased. Among 16,213 examined workers (mean age 43.5 years; 83.2% male), the detection rate of abnormal pulmonary function was 8.7% and that of high-frequency hearing loss was 18.8%; the detection rate of hearing loss increased progressively over the years before declining in 2025. Multivariable logistic regression showed that male sex and older age were associated with both outcomes. Workers in state-owned and private enterprises had higher odds of abnormal pulmonary function (OR = 2.20 and 2.61, respectively), and the odds increased with enterprise size (OR = 1.77–2.48). For high-frequency hearing loss, workers with ≥10 years of service (OR = 1.15) and those employed in rock drilling, transportation, and flotation positions had significantly elevated odds (OR = 4.71, 2.81, and 1.91, respectively). Conclusion Supervision of noise and dust must be continuously strengthened, particularly in micro-enterprises. Optimizing engineering controls and raising awareness of personal protection are essential for reducing the risk of occupational diseases.

items.title: Occupational Hazards and Personal Protective Equipment Interventions Relevant to Environmental Health Practitioners in Government Regulatory Services: A Systematic Review of Direct and Indirect Evidence
items.abstract: Environmental Health Practitioners (EHPs) undertake regulatory, inspection and field-based activities that may expose them to multiple occupational hazards. Although personal protective equipment (PPE) is an important occupational risk-control measure, evidence concerning its effectiveness specifically among EHPs remains limited. The study aims to synthesise and evaluate available evidence on occupational hazards and the effectiveness of PPE interventions relevant to EHPs working in government regulatory services. A systematic review was conducted and reported according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Various Research platforms were searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2000 and March 2026. Studies involving EHPs and related regulatory professionals were included, together with relevant evidence from comparable occupational groups where the hazards, exposure pathways or PPE interventions applied to environmental health practice. Due to heterogeneity in study designs, populations, PPE interventions and outcomes, findings were synthesised narratively. Thirty-four unique studies were included. Biological hazards were most frequently reported (82.4%), followed by chemical (47.1%), physical (44.1%), psychosocial (32.4%), organisational/workplace (26.5%), climate/environmental (17.6%) and radiation hazards (2.9%). Respiratory protection was the most frequently reported PPE category (70.6%), followed by gloves (55.9%), protective clothing (41.2%), eye/face protection (35.3%) and protective footwear (20.6%). Overall, appropriately selected PPE reduced occupational exposure; however, effectiveness varied by PPE type and occupational context and was influenced by availability, training, knowledge, adherence, comfort, correct donning and doffing, contamination control, and organisational support. Of the 34 studies, only three directly investigated EHPs, Environmental Health Officers, or Public Health Inspectors. PPE is an important component of occupational protection for EHPs but should be selected according to the specific hazard, task and exposure route and implemented within a broader occupational risk-management approach. The limited direct evidence among environmental health regulatory professionals highlights the need for EHP-specific research to inform PPE guidelines, training and occupational health policies.

items.title: On the Role of Boundary Objects in Agentic Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence involve deploying agents that execute tasks and coordinate with one another to produce outputs. These agents, to an extent, mimic human behavior in terms of the need for coordination, in which the output of one agent is used by other agents. The use of agentic AI further underscores the need to verify each agent and their interim outputs to build trustworthiness and ensure reliable final outputs. In relation to these three areas, the use of artifacts plays an important role, as they can manifest and communicate outputs in a comprehensible manner. These artifacts serve as boundary objects, facilitating knowledge integration and the creation of a common understanding among agents and humans. Boundary object theory can therefore provide a useful lens for understanding agent-to-agent interactions, agent-to-human interactions, and, finally, human-to-human interactions based on the agents’ outputs. In this paper, we present a boundary object perspective that sheds light on facilitating interactions within both technical and sociotechnical systems. We leverage previous research on circular ecosystems to contextualize our discussion, contribute to both agentic AI and boundary object theory, and provide novel insights into the implications of transdisciplinary engineering for the use of agentic AI in complex sociotechnical systems.

items.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
items.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

items.title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

items.title: Optimizing Query Decomposition for Reliable Validation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made querying databases more accessible, but cannot guarantee that the SQL they generate is correct. Without a trusted reference query, a validator (human or LLM) must decide whether a generated query answers the intended question. Enterprise questions often require queries with multiple joins, nested subqueries, and multi-level aggregation, and validating such a query in one judgment is error-prone. Decomposition simplifies this task by rewriting a query into smaller queries (blocks) that recompose to the original, each checked against its own sub-question. Decompositions differ, however: smaller blocks make each judgment easier but require more judgments, and the best balance depends on the validator's ability. We formulate validation-aware query decomposition as an optimization problem. Just as a query optimizer chooses among equivalent plans by estimated cost, we choose among decompositions by how reliably a given validator is expected to check them. We model how task difficulty and validator ability jointly affect reliability and define an objective that balances reliability against the number of judgments. Over a space of decompositions derived from logical-plan rewrites, our search finds an optimal one. We implement it in DecoVal, a pipeline that presents each block with its sub-question and input interface, combines local verdicts into a query-level decision, and localizes errors to blocks. A user study shows that decomposition helps human validators catch and locate errors: with DecoVal, participants caught 91% of the errors, up from 36% without decomposition, and located the error in nearly every rejection. Experiments on BEAVER and Spider 2.0 with LLM validators show that DecoVal also raises error-detection recall over whole-query validation while keeping precision high, and that the best granularity depends on the validator.

items.title: Pathwise-Budgeted LLM Routing: Online Allocation with K-Bit Tail-Cost Learning
items.abstract: Firms using large language models under fixed budgets must decide which model to call and whether to retry a failed task. Because a call's charge is revealed only after completion, one long response can exhaust the remaining budget and leave later tasks unserved. Our objective is to maximize the number of tasks solved before service stops. We develop a contextual bandit policy, ADP-HT, which learns each model's task-specific success probability and constructs conservative cost estimates from coarsened response-length labels on a quantile grid with $2^K$ intervals. The policy weighs predicted success against these costs, adjusting the cost penalty to realized spending and the budget available per remaining task. Under calibration, local regularity, and grid-coverage conditions, we bound the excess allowance in the policy's conservative cost estimates. At a fixed sample size, increasing $K$ reduces the discretization term but increases the estimation allowance. At the tightest tested budgets, ADP-HT solves more than twice as many MATH500 and GPQA tasks as the best implemented baseline. It achieves the highest mean cumulative score at ten of fourteen RouterBench budgets. On LiveCodeBench, it outperforms a deployed commercial router in both default and cost-saving modes at the three lowest test budgets.

items.abstract: The use of learning media is an integral component in the instructional design of Islamic Religious Education (IRE) to bridge abstract concepts into concrete ones and create a joyful learning environment. However, its implementation still faces obstacles, such as teachers' limited digital literacy, uneven school infrastructure, administrative burdens, and challenges in visualizing theological materials without diminishing the sacredness of religious teachings. This study examines the concepts, problems, impacts, and optimization strategies of media in IRE instruction. The findings indicate that the use of varied and interactive media significantly impacts students' interest, intrinsic motivation, and active participation. Key solutions to overcome these challenges include continuous professional development for digital competence, flexibility in infrastructure utilization, the implementation of educational gamification approaches, and strict content curation to maintain the accuracy of religious substances.

items.title: PharmacoMicrobiology and PharmacoMicrobioResistance: Expanding the Paradigm of Drug-Microbe Interactions and Resistance Beyond Antimicrobials in the Pharmacosphere
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is framed as a defining global health crisis, yet its conceptual boundaries remain artificially narrow. By focusing primarily on antibiotics, current paradigms ignore a broader reality: microorganisms continuously respond to the full spectrum of human and animal pharmaceuticals in both patients and the environment. This oversight obscures critical dimensions of drug action and resistance mechanisms. We propose PharmacoMicrobiology (PM) and PharmacoMicrobioResistance (PMR) to redefine microbial–drug interactions beyond traditional antimicrobials, specifically accounting for multiple simultaneous drug exposures. Microbes actively transform, degrade, and resist diverse non-antibiotic drugs, potentially undermining therapeutic efficacy across multiple distinct medical fields. Shaped by environmental contamination, microbiome dynamics, and horizontal gene transfer, resistance to these non-antibiotic drugs may already be emerging entirely unnoticed. Ignoring this expanded resistome risks repeating past failures. Integrating PM and PMR into comprehensive One Health frameworks, powered by advanced artificial intelligence, is essential to anticipate, detect, and prevent drug resistance.

items.title: Physicians Assign Themselves More Responsibility Than the General Population when AI Fails in Healthcare: A Swedish Cross-Sectional Survey
items.abstract: Abstract Background: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into clinical decision-making creates uncertainty regarding responsibility and accountability when adverse outcomes occur. Despite this, data regarding stakeholder perspectives remain scarce, especially quantitative data comparing physician and public views on responsibility allocation and transparency. This study aims to evaluate and compare how physicians and the general population in Sweden attribute responsibility for negative medical outcomes when AI is used to support healthcare decisions in primary care, as well as their views on the necessity of transparently disclosing AI use to patients.Methods: A nationwide, cross-sectional, mixed-methods survey was conducted in Sweden between February and May 2025. The survey targeted two distinct cohorts (N = 500 per group): licensed physicians under 70 years, sampled from the National Board of Health and Welfare register, and adults aged 18 or older sampled from the Swedish population registry. The survey used case vignettes as background for multiple-choice questions, with complementary open-ended free-text responses. The data was evaluated using comparative statistical analysis and reflexive thematic analysis.Results: Physicians were significantly more likely than the general population to assign responsibility to the physician (92\% vs. 74\%) and to favor a shared responsibility model involving the physician (48\% vs. 35\%). In contrast, the general population more frequently selected non-physician actor combinations (26\% vs. 8\%) and assigned greater responsibility to the patient in a scenario involving direct patient-AI interaction without a physician involved. Neither group broadly assigned responsibility to the AI itself (1.3\% physicians vs. 10\% general population). The reflexive thematic analysis reinforced these results, identifying a shared accountability framework where all actors share responsibility, but where the physician serves as the ultimate safeguard. A majority of the general population (68\%) affirmed the patient's right to always know if AI was used, in contrast to only 23\% of physicians who exhibited a polarised distribution. Conclusion: Respondents endorse a shared responsibility model among actors involved in implementing and using AI for medical decisions. The physician is viewed as the essential human-in-the-loop, bearing ultimate accountability for adverse outcomes of AI-assisted medical decisions according to a vast majority of respondents. Divergent perspectives regarding transparency emphasise the need to clarify informed consent standards for AI deployment in healthcare.

items.title: PixelBench: Evaluating Language Models for Pixel-Art Creation
items.abstract: Pixel art is widely used in games and digital content creation, requiring readable forms, coherent spatial relationships, and harmonious colors under limited resolution and palette constraints. Language models show growing promise in visual creation, yet their pixel art creation capabilities lack systematic evaluation. We introduce PixelBench, formalizing text-to-image generation and instruction-guided editing for pixel art and providing a benchmark for these tasks. We further present a creation environment in which language model agents invoke drawing tools through code to generate and edit pixel art. We assess the quality of generated artwork through human evaluation and employ a multimodal large language model as a judge, validating the agreement between its automated assessments and human preferences. We compare language models and configurations across diverse subjects and canvas sizes. In our experiments, GPT-6 Astra achieves both the highest average judge score and the best average human rank, highlighting the potential of general-purpose language models for pixel art creation. We release the tasks, all artworks, the human rankings, and the judge protocol.

items.title: PONTE: Personalized Orchestration for Natural Language Trustworthy Explanations
items.abstract: Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) seeks to enhance the transparency and accountability of machine learning systems, yet most methods follow a one-size-fits-all paradigm that neglects user differences in expertise, goals, and cognitive needs. Although Large Language Models can translate technical explanations into natural language, they introduce challenges related to faithfulness and hallucinations. To address these challenges, we present PONTE ( P ersonalized O rchestration for N atural language T rustworthy E xplanations), a human-in-the-loop framework for adaptive and reliable XAI narratives. PONTE models personalization as a closed-loop validation and adaptation process rather than prompt engineering. It combines: (i) a low-dimensional preference model capturing stylistic requirements; (ii) a preference-conditioned generator grounded in structured XAI artifacts; and (iii) verification modules enforcing numerical faithfulness, informational completeness, and stylistic alignment, optionally supported by retrieval-grounded argumentation. User feedback iteratively updates the preference state, enabling quick personalization. Automatic and human evaluations across healthcare and finance domains show that the verification–refinement loop substantially improves completeness and stylistic alignment over validation-free generation. Human studies further confirm strong agreement between intended preference vectors and perceived style, robustness to generation stochasticity, and consistently positive quality assessments.

items.title: Practices of Human-AI Collaboration in Enterprise Generative AI Adoption and Their Implications for Organisational Digital Innovation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is beginning to be used in enterprise workflows as a flexible generator of text, code, images, summaries, and conversations. However, the organisation's value is not derived from technology alone. This conceptual paper explores how enterprises can organise human-AI collaboration during the adoption process and what such practices may achieve for digital innovation. Differentiate among support, sequential co-creation, iterative co-creation and supervised delegation; link these models to workflow redesign, knowledge sharing, service improvement and innovation capabilities. Based on the above discussion, the conditions for converting model outputs into responsible organisational behaviour are task decomposition, verification, role clarity, learning routines and governance. It will also solve hallucination, bias, confidentiality, deskilling, over-reliance and unequal participation. No original data, field research, experiments or performance tests were conducted. Therefore, this paper provides mechanisms and practice-oriented suggestions instead of causal results. It believes that generative AI should be treated as a fallible organisational participant in sociotechnical arrangements, and people are responsible for the goals, contextual judgement, verification and consequential decisions.

items.title: PRELIMINARY ERGONOMIC ANALYSIS OF HEALTHCARE PROFESSIONALS’ WORKING CONDITIONS IN A BRAZILIAN UNIVERSITY HOSPITAL EMERGENCY UNIT
items.abstract: This study analyzed the working conditions of healthcare professionals in the emergency and urgency unit of a Brazilian University Hospital using a preliminary ergonomic analysis. The method comprised two tools: the Ergonomic Checklist and the Self-Assessment Tool Ergonomics/Human Factors questionnaire. These instruments facilitated the assessment of physical, cognitive, and organizational demands within the occupational environment. The findings highlighted critical ergonomic issues, such as inadequate furniture, excessive noise, and poor lighting conditions. A high level of physical strain was noted due to the intense work pace and constant movement required, while cognitive demands were marked by time pressure, mental overload, and emotional stress. Organizational deficiencies, particularly those related to communication, were also identified as factors compromising task execution and workplace safety. The study underscores the need for ergonomic interventions, including workload adjustments, planned breaks, environmental adaptations, psychological support programs, and improved internal communication strategies. These measures aim to reduce physical and cognitive strain, promote healthier and safer working conditions, and improve the quality of patient care. Moreover, the proposed method can be systematically applied to other hospital units to determine whether the identified demands are specific to the studied unit or indicative of broader systemic challenges within the hospital environment.

items.title: Premise Recovery in Software Design: What Does This Decision Rest On?
items.abstract: Design decisions shape software architecture, and writing them down preserves the reasons behind it. Architecture decision records (ADRs) capture them, each with its context, choice, and consequences. A decision can depend on earlier ones: reversing one of them would force its review. We call these its premises. Yet ADRs do not always name their premises. When a decision is reversed, engineers supersede its ADR and search by hand for what it affects. That search can miss ADRs resting on an unnamed premise. We frame this as premise recovery: given an ADR with identifiers masked, find its premises among earlier records. We collect 1,060 ADRs from 36 repositories and label 1,529 candidate pairs for 60 target ADRs. Two LLM annotators agree at \k{appa} = 0.859. An independent human annotator, blind to their labels, agrees with the stated/implicit tag on 30 of 32 premises (\k{appa} = 0.875). We compare 7 open-weight models with 2 baselines that use no LLM. Qwen3.8-27B reaches F1 0.756, against 0.466 for word overlap; 2 models added post hoc score similarly. On the 11 premises whose titles barely overlap the target, it finds 0.758, while word overlap finds none. Reasoning raises its recall of implicit premises but not its F1. Word overlap with as many predictions gains 69% as much. We find only 2 to 3 stale dependents, though we searched for unlinked ones in only 30 of 66 supersessions. Open models could thus suggest unwritten premises when a decision is reversed, with precision between 0.68 and 0.78.

items.title: Preparing Students for the Realities of Contemporary Nursing Requires More Than Teaching Communication Models or Human-Factors Theory
items.abstract: Preparing students for the realities of contemporary nursing requires more than teaching communication models or human-factors theory. It demands learning experiences that reveal how individuals behave under pressure, ambiguity, and cognitive strain. This presentation showcases “Party Quirks”, an improvisation-based simulation that creates a controlled but deliberately chaotic environment in which students experience the emotional and behavioural challenges associated with real clinical practice. Unlike high-fidelity clinical simulation, this activity uses social unpredictability as its realism. Students must navigate unclear communication, disruptive behaviours, conflicting cues, and rising frustration while working collaboratively to solve a shared problem. These features reflect well-documented contributors to human error in healthcare such as hierarchical inhibition, task fixation, reluctance to escalate concerns, and the cognitive overload described in patient safety literature (NHS Patient Safety Strategy, 2019; Reason, 2000). The design mirrors the uncertainty and mental load that nurses routinely encounter, from unexpected interruptions to ambiguous team communication. Across multiple cohorts, “Party Quirks” has produced high engagement, rich reflective discussion, and immediate behavioural insight. Students consistently report recognising their own tendencies under pressure, including avoidance of help-seeking, overanalysis, communication breakdowns, and emotional reactions they had not anticipated. These reflections closely echo the human-factors themes explored in clinical incident analysis and safety training. The structured debrief links students’ in-game behaviours to real-world scenarios, promoting discussion around psychological safety, speaking up, situational awareness, emotional intelligence, and team dynamics. The activity has also demonstrated inclusivity benefits, offering a low-stakes, culturally flexible space in which diverse learners contribute meaningfully to teamwork and communication tasks. This session will present the design, theoretical rationale, implementation guidance, and observed outcomes of “Party Quirks”. It argues that low-resource, high-impact gamified simulations can meaningfully enhance the preparedness of nursing, midwifery, and allied health students by allowing them to feel and examine the human factors that shape safe clinical practice.

items.title: Progressive Layer-wise Supervision: Deep-to-Shallow Supervision Annealing for Efficient and Robust Speech Deepfake Detection
items.abstract: Speech foundation models pretrained via self-supervised learning provide powerful representations for deepfake detection, yet we find that standard fine-tuning exploits only the deepest transformer layers-leaving the majority of the network's capacity discriminatively inert. Layer-wise probing of XLS-R-128 reveals that the top two-thirds of the transformer stack contribute negligibly to anti-spoofing performance after standard fine-tuning, a phenomenon we term shallow-layer dormancy. We connect this observation to the representational redundancy of pretrained transformers: adjacent layers encode highly similar information, and fine-tuning without explicit intermediate supervision reinforces rather than breaks this redundancy. To address this, we propose Progressive Layer-wise Supervision (PLS), a training framework that attaches a shared linear classifier to every transformer layer and schedules layer-wise loss contributions via an exponentially annealed power weighting. Early training concentrates supervision on deep layers to preserve the pretrained representational hierarchy; later training progressively redistributes supervision to shallower layers, converting dormant earlier representations into discriminative ones. Competitive detection (<9.25% average EER) is achievable on XLS-R-128 at layer 7, which reduces the parameter count from 315M to 101M and exemplifies an early exit mechanism. Experiments across twelve benchmarks spanning in-domain, and out-of-domain deepfake scenarios show PLS achieves a new state-of-the-art with 239M parameters, outperforming prior methods with larger and more complex architectures.

items.title: PromptPoseFX: Authoring Pose-Driven Visual Effects through Augmented Prompting and Interactive Refinement
items.abstract: Human pose-driven visual effects offer a compelling way for enhancing video expressiveness and storytelling. Authoring such effects with traditional video editing tools is a complex and time-consuming task that requires considerable technical expertise and manual effort. While generative AI models can simplify the workflow by reducing manual scripting through language-driven generation, existing approaches suffer from imprecise alignment between visual effects and pose data, failure to preserve original video content, and limited support for fine-grained, iterative refinement. To address these challenges, we present PromptPoseFX, an interactive system that allows creators to author pose-driven visual effects through augmented language prompts and interactive refinement. Our system leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to translate high-level user intent into parameterized procedural graphics scripts, automatically mapping pose-tracking data to specific effect parameters, allowing precise alignment with human motion. This script-based approach manages effects as independent layers, thereby preserving the original content of the underlying video. To reduce language ambiguity, our interface offers controls across spatial, temporal, and parameter domains, enabling the precise, intuitive, and iterative authoring of pose-driven visual effects. We evaluated PromptPoseFX through a comparative study against a text-only LLM interface, followed by an exploratory study. In the comparative study, participants rated PromptPoseFX significantly higher than the text-only baseline on measures of perceived control and precision. The exploratory study examined usability and creativity support in open-ended authoring tasks.

items.title: Proposed new words and collective identity in human and language model agent groups
items.abstract: Abstract Groups develop distinctive words even when ordinary expressions are sufficient. Such words can symbolize collective identity, and observational studies link language use to community attachment. We examined identity change in temporary groups of one human and four disclosed large language model (LLM) agents, comparing discussions with and without a neologism proposal across recruitment waves. We recruited 100 Japanese participants in two sequential waves; an agent proposed a new word only in the first wave. Mean collective identity change did not differ significantly between waves. Within the proposal wave, favorable ratings of the proposed word were associated with change in identity, but this association did not survive correction for multiple testing (adjusted $$p=0.229$$ ). The three-way interaction among recruitment wave, message count, and team impression had a nominal $$p=0.027$$ but did not survive correction (adjusted $$p=0.082$$ ). In a sensitivity analysis, the interaction was not significant after adjustment for midpoint identity (nominal $$p=0.078$$ ; adjusted $$p=0.624$$ ). The nonsignificant between-wave comparison and exploratory associations that did not survive correction, together with wave confounding and post-discussion evaluations, limit causal inference and motivate randomized studies with repeated measures to test whether proposed group language affects identification.

items.title: Psychological Readiness for the Green Energy Transition: A Human-Factors Model for Aviation Maintenance Crews
items.abstract: Green-aviation research on battery and alternative-fuel chemistries has advanced rapidly, but a persistent blind spot remains: the psychological readiness of the maintenance personnel who operate these systems daily under safety-critical conditions.Silver-zinc (Ag-Zn) batteries, used in fighter aircraft for their high energy density, evolve hydrogen and oxygen gas through electrolysis of their alkaline electrolyte during charging -a hazard that builds invisibly over 36-to-72-hour charge cycles and becomes dangerous only once hydrogen concentration crosses its lower explosion limit.Managing this hazard depends less on chemistry knowledge and more on sustained technician vigilance during a long, low-stimulation monitoring task -precisely the condition under which classic vigilancedecrement research shows attentional lapses emerge, independent of training or competence.Drawing on the author's two decades as an aviation electrical maintenance engineer and a second career in applied and clinical psychology within the same defence environment, this paper argues that emerging green-energy-storage chemistries (lithium-ion, solidstate, hydrogen fuel cells) will introduce comparable low-visibility, highconsequence hazards, and that maintenance-crew psychological readiness must be engineered alongside the chemistry itself.Integrating self-efficacy theory, the Technology Acceptance Model, and vigilance-decrement research, the paper proposes a Psychology-Chemistry Interface Model with three components -chemistry-literacy calibration, hazardtolerability screening, and stress-buffered reporting culture -and a training framework for building calibrated, sustained vigilance in ground crews adopting new energy chemistries, including a low-cost toolkit -a pre-task hazard card, a vigilance-rotation roster, a hazard-tolerability selfcheck, and an added prompt within existing incident-reporting procedures -deployable at a single maintenance unit without new infrastructure.

items.title: PSYCHOPHYSIOLOGICAL DEVELOPMENT CHARACTERISTICS OF PRIMARY SCHOOL STUDENTS AND THE ROLE OF PLAY ACTIVITIES IN ENHANCING THEIR COGNITIVE ENGAGEMENT
items.abstract: The psychophysiological development of primary school children is fundamental for their academic success, yet the systematic integration of play to enhance cognitive engagement, especially its specific mechanisms, remains understudied. The aim of this study is to investigate primary school children's psychophysiological development and play's role in enhancing cognitive engagement. This article explores the intricate link between psychophysiological maturation—including brain development, motor skills, sensory processing, and emotional regulation—and cognitive engagement. It examines how these developmental trajectories influence learning and how play-based strategies can bridge developmental gaps. The text highlights that rapid brain development, particularly in the prefrontal cortex, enhances executive functions, inhibitory control, working memory, and cognitive flexibility. It emphasizes that myelination improves neural transmission, while refined motor and sensory skills, alongside evolving emotional regulation, are crucial for sustained attention and active participation. Understanding these developmental aspects is vital for educators to tailor learning experiences that optimize children's potential for cognitive engagement and academic success through effective pedagogical approaches.

items.title: Reading Royalty Risk at Scale: LLM-Assisted Construction and Reliability Analysis of an Offset- and-Deduction Clause Corpus from SEC-Filed Technology Licences
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce RODEO , a corpus of 5,111 royalty offset and deduction clause spans from material-contract exhibits filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (709 exhibits, 417 filers), labelled for their economic function under a seven-function taxonomy. Because exhaustive human annotation is costly, we build the resource with a protocol assisted by a large language model (LLM): independent double classification, adjudication of substantive disagreements, and a stratified human spot-check. We release the corpus with source identifiers and privacy-screened excerpts, together with the per-pass and adjudicated labels, prompts and code. As a quality-control analysis we examine how far the model can be trusted. It is highly self-consistent on the surface (82.4% exact-set agreement across passes) yet poorly calibrated: 82% of predictions carry the maximal confidence score, even that top bin flips label across passes 13.8% of the time, and the model’s own uncertainty flag recovers only 1% of genuine disagreements. On a deliberately hard subset, a model from an independent family agrees with the adjudicated label only 36.6% of the time, whereas on a broad stratified sample the two LLM annotators agree substantially (macro Cohen’s κ = 0.78). Inter-pass disagreement, not self-reported confidence, is therefore the more useful signal for triaging hard cases when full human labelling is infeasible. Supervised baselines show that the labelling is learnable (a bag-of-words logistic-regression classifier reaches macro-F1 0.80; the notice-and-documentation condition is hardest). The released labels are LLM-generated with a human spot-check (“silver”), and we set out the path to a fully human-adjudicated version.

items.title: REEL: Brain-Guided Video Generation and Selection by Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear Decoding from fMRI data
items.abstract: Visual brain decoding from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data has made remarkable progress in recent years, driven by increasingly powerful artificial intelligence (AI) models and the growing availability of large-scale public datasets. However, despite the impressive advances achieved in static image decoding, the reconstruction of videos from fMRI signals remains challenging due to the temporal mismatch between rapidly changing video stimuli and the slow dynamics of the blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) response. We evaluate a Bayesian-inspired proposal-and-rerank strategy on CC2017 and the BOLD Moments Dataset (BMD), using a linear semantic decoder, a pretrained video generator, and three neural encoding streams with ridge readouts and learned pooling in two streams. We refer to this framework as REEL (Reranking Encoder Embeddings with Linear decoding). Compared with a single generated candidate, reranking increases mean Video 50-way accuracy from 0.2359 to 0.2434 across three CC2017 participants and from 0.3653 to 0.3920 across ten BMD participants. These findings suggest an alternative and conceptually simpler strategy for improving video brain decoding, highlighting the potential of our approach as a complementary direction to increasingly complex pipelines.

items.title: Reflective, Experiential and Coaching-Based Workplace Learning in Service Organisations A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Service organisations depend on frontline employees whose competence is built largely at work, yet evidence on structured workplace learning remains fragmented. This systematic literature review synthesises empirical evidence on reflective, experiential and coaching-based learning among in-service workers and identifies the organisational conditions that shape it. Following PRISMA 2020, 97 open-access journal articles published between 2021 and 2026 were retrieved from Scopus and screened against set eligibility criteria. Twenty-nine studies were included, appraised with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool and synthesised thematically. The evidence was dominated by healthcare and human services in high-income countries, qualitative designs and self-reported outcomes. Five themes emerged, (1) reflection works best when built into daily work; (2) real work experience builds skills when it matches the job; (3) coaching and feedback depend on prepared coaches and trust; (4) peers and groups spread new practice across teams; and (5) workplace conditions, such as supervisor support, psychological safety, hierarchy and workload, decide whether learning is used. The review proposes a structured workplace learning cycle linking these elements. Workplace learning becomes sustainable when it is built into daily work and supported by supervisors. Stronger behavioural evidence is needed from Southeast Asian and frontline service sectors such as private security.

items.title: RemeshingAgent: An Iterative Agent for Repair-Based Decimation of Generated Building Meshes
items.abstract: Aggressively simplifying a generated high-poly building mesh to 0.5-1% of its faces confronts a hard limit. The surface looks complete, yet the mesh is topologically shattered: 10^3-10^4 connected components and non-manifold thin walls. Below a certain budget, every practical decimator "melts": it deletes parts, welds thin walls, or breaks the error tolerance. We attribute this to instance-specific pathology: which components are significant and where the cliff sits vary from mesh to mesh, so no single fixed algorithm suffices, and decimation becomes an iterative loop of cleaning, simplifying, and verifying. We present RemeshingAgent, an agent that turns this loop into a validated process. The melting follows from a triangle-budget decomposition into curvature, crease, component, and genus terms: below the component floor, no output satisfies the repair contract, and cleaning first is the theory-mandated response. At a 0.5% budget the agent stays topology-clean where QEM and vertex clustering melt, matches a commercial remesher on 20 unseen city buildings, and on the 24 training buildings a nine-participant single-workstation blind study prefers our outputs 168:48 (p = 0.0195, subject-level sign test). The trained skill deploys as retrieval replay: 11.7 seconds per mesh on CPU, with no LLM calls.

items.title: Research on the Knowledge Transformation of Educational Discourse on Short-Video Platforms and the Cognitive Engagement Pathways of Learners
items.abstract: With the development of mobile internet, short video platforms have become important venues for knowledge dissemination and learning, significantly impacting traditional modes of educational discourse production and communication. This study takes educational discourse on short video platforms as its research subject, focusing on knowledge transformation mechanisms and learners' cognitive engagement processes. By integrating literature review, content analysis, and case studies, it comprehensively examines the patterns through which knowledge evolves from implicit to explicit and from specialized to popular within short video education contexts. Educational discourse on short video platforms is characterized by fragmentation, visuality, and interactivity. Knowledge transformation primarily occurs through discourse simplification, contextual embedding, emotional activation, and symbolic reconstruction. Creators employ narrative techniques and visual language to reduce the complexity of knowledge, making abstract concepts more accessible. Meanwhile, learners' cognitive engagement is diverse and multi-faceted, involving attention capture, information processing, meaning construction, and knowledge transfer—manifested in social behaviors such as commenting, liking, and sharing—which can either positively or negatively influence deep learning. Furthermore, there exists an interactive relationship among platform algorithms, content creators’ professionalism, and learners’ self-regulation abilities: while algorithms enhance accessibility to knowledge, they may also lead to superficial cognition and echo chambers. Based on these findings, this paper offers recommendations for improving the creation of educational content on short video platforms, including enhancing content quality and authenticity, building interactive cognitive scaffolds, and improving learners’ media literacy. These suggestions aim to provide insights and support for maximizing the educational potential of short video platforms and promoting learners’ cognitive development, thereby contributing to the healthy growth of informal learning in the digital age.

items.title: Rethinking Feature Selection: A Fair-Division Approach Under Model Uncertainty
items.abstract: Feature selection, also known as variable selection, is a foundational problem in econometrics, artificial intelligence, and machine learning. However, widely used procedures may be inaccurate, unstable under collinearity, and sensitive to sampling noise and may lack a principled interpretation in terms of how they allocate explanatory power. This paper develops a feature-selection framework that extends a fair-division approach introduced by Hu ([2020, 2025). We represent the explanatory or forecasting performance of feature subsets as payoffs in a coalitional game subject to sampling uncertainty. Candidate features are partitioned into selected and unselected sets according to their fair-division values, defined using a modified Shapley value. Model uncertainty is represented by a beta-binomial distribution over subset size and a uniform distribution over subsets conditional on size. Each feature’s value combines the expected marginal gain from inclusion with the expected opportunity loss associated with exclusion, thereby treating all candidates symmetrically ex ante under a veil-of-ignorance principle. We further propose a sequential selection algorithm that uses a Monte Carlo approximation and a likelihood-ratio screening rule that admits at most one feature per iteration. Across the simulation designs considered, the procedure attains substantially higher exact-identification rates than those of the benchmark methods, including stepwise, unidirectional, GETS-style, and LASSO-based procedures. The paper also examines residual-share-based hyperparameter calibration, computational complexity, selection consistency, and practical implementation considerations.

items.title: Rethinking Social Sustainability Metrics in Chile’s Lithium Sociotechnical Transition: Numbers, Policies and Knowledge
items.abstract: Social sustainability indicators are central decision-support tools in mining, used to evaluate social performance and guide policy and investment. However, these indicators do not merely describe reality; they actively shape it by defining what is measured, reported, and governed. In the context of lithium extraction from brines, this performative role becomes particularly relevant as expanding production and technological changes reconfigure water use, territorial relations, and community livelihoods in sensitive ecosystems such as the high-Andean salt flats of Chile, which host some of the world’s largest lithium reserves and production sites. This paper analyses how social sustainability is currently measured in the lithium industry and identifies the opportunities and limitations of existing indicator frameworks. Using a systematic analysis of sustainability reports and international reporting standards, combined with insights from stakeholder interviews, we examine the indicators commonly used to assess lithium extraction activities. The results show that existing indicator systems are structured by global reporting standards and compliance-oriented metrics, whilst territorial dynamics and relational aspects of social sustainability remain partially captured. Based on these results, the paper discusses implications for the design of social sustainability indicators in critical mineral extraction. We argue that improving sustainability assessment requires incorporating territorially situated perspectives, ecosystem-based knowledge, and broader participation of communities, universities, public institutions, and firms. In this sense, redesigning sustainability indicators as more reflexive and participatory tools may support more socially robust pathways in the sociotechnical transition of the lithium industry in Chile.

items.title: Rethinking the satisfaction–turnover intention link: the role of transformational leadership
items.abstract: Purpose The study tests the explanatory power of a satisfaction-centred account of transformational leadership and turnover intention in a Turkish corporate sample in a national context commonly characterised as relatively collectivist and high in power distance. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on psychological contract theory and the job characteristics model, the study analyses survey responses from 884 employees representing Generations X, Y and Z. Transformational leadership is operationalised through a brief, responsibility-oriented five-item measure capturing idealised influence, inspirational motivation and intellectual stimulation. Findings Transformational leadership was positively associated with job satisfaction and explained incremental variance beyond the five job characteristics. The hypothesised indirect association through job satisfaction was not supported. Generation moderated the leadership–satisfaction association, with a significantly stronger slope for Generation Z than for Generations X and Y, although the indirect association through job satisfaction did not differ significantly across cohorts. Practical implications Organisations should not assume that initiatives designed solely to enhance job satisfaction will fully account for turnover intention. Leadership development and job design appear to make distinct and complementary contributions to employees' work experience, while the stronger leadership–satisfaction association observed for Generation Z warrants attention without implying wholly separate generational management systems. Originality/value The study tests the explanatory reach of a satisfaction-centred account of transformational leadership and turnover intention in a collectivistic, high power-distance setting. It shows that the transformational leadership behaviours captured by the measure retain incremental explanatory value beyond job characteristics, while the expected indirect association through satisfaction is not supported and generational moderation is concentrated in the Generation Z contrast.

items.title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
items.abstract: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce. Within repositories, no specification detects a difference. LLM intent classifiers agree with human labels about as well as two humans agree with each other, whereas keyword rules do not (kappa = 0.69 to 0.72 against 0.38), and the two reach different verdicts on why agent code is modified. Humans make most modifications to agent code under every unit and window. Re-run on our data, five published designs each change their result with a single choice. Whether agent code survives longer than human code is therefore decided as much by the measurement as by the code. We derive an operationalization checklist for post-merge studies.

items.title: Revisiting warranting theory in AI-mediated communication: An evaluation of writer and source effects in online reviews.
items.abstract: This article examines how attributing the actual writer of an online message to artificial intelligence (AI) , rather than a human, shapes impression formation . By drawing on and extending warranting theory, this article examines how source role labels (self vs. third party) and content writer labels (AI vs. human) interact to affect impression formation and message effects in the context of hotel reviews. Two preregistered experiments (Study 1: N = 461; Study 2: N = 444) found that, for the same positive hotel review, third-party reviewers were perceived more favorably than self-reviewers (i.e., hotel managers), leading to more positive evaluations of the hotel. Reviews attributed to AI writers negatively impacted impressions of the reviewer and diminished the review’s impact, with third-party reviewers more negatively affected by AI writer labels than self-reviewers. AI labels of user-generated content, therefore, attenuate the effects of source role and move people out of their default impression formation state. We demonstrate theoretical advancements for warranting theory and AI-mediated communication.

items.title: RFAmpDesigner: A Two-Level LLM-guided Optimization Framework for Automated Differential CMOS RF Amplifier Sizing
items.abstract: Automated RF amplifier sizing is challenging because the design process is inherently hierarchical, the parameter space is high-dimensional and strongly coupled, and high-fidelity circuit simulation is expensive. Conventional optimization and reinforcement learning methods typically require many iterations and make limited use of RF domain knowledge, making them costly under tight simulation budgets. Large language models (LLMs) provide broad prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but are unreliable for direct numerical optimization. This paper presents RFAmpDesigner, a two-level optimization framework for automated schematic-level sizing of differential CMOS RF amplifiers. At the outer level, the circuit-parameter space is abstracted into a resource-allocation space, where LLMs make high-level allocation decisions and adjust them according to feedback from the inner level. At the inner level, RF design knowledge is used to decompose the flat sizing problem into a sequence of low-dimensional subproblems. Conventional optimizers then solve these subproblems to find circuit implementations consistent with the assigned resources. This structure allows numerical optimizers to focus on low-dimensional searches in the circuit-parameter space, while the LLM reasons and acts over a physically meaningful design space using simulation feedback. The main evaluation covers low-noise amplifier (LNA), driver amplifier (DA), and power amplifier (PA) designs within the target differential CMOS RF amplifier family. Experimental results show that it achieves a higher success rate under a limited simulation budget in both easy and hard regimes.

items.title: ROBOTIC-ASSISTED SURGERY IN MODERN HEALTHCARE: CLINICAL EFFECTIVENESS, ECONOMIC ACCESSIBILITY, AND SOCIETAL IMPLICATIONS OF THE DA VINCI SURGICAL SYSTEM
items.abstract: Background: Robotic-assisted surgery has become an increasingly prominent component of modern healthcare, with the da Vinci Surgical System representing one of the most widely adopted platforms. Despite its technological advantages, including enhanced instrument articulation, three-dimensional visualization, and improved surgical ergonomics, questions remain regarding its comparative clinical effectiveness, economic accessibility, and broader implications for healthcare systems. Aim: This review critically examines the available evidence concerning the clinical outcomes and economic implications of da Vinci-assisted procedures compared with conventional laparoscopic and open surgery. Materials and Methods: Particular attention is given to operative time, postoperative complications, hospital stay, surgical conversion rates, and healthcare expenditure. The review also considers the influence of institutional resources, surgical expertise, and technological accessibility on the implementation of robotic-assisted procedures. Results: Recent comparative studies indicate that robotic surgery may offer advantages in selected surgical settings; however, these benefits are not consistently demonstrated across all procedures and patient populations. Furthermore, substantial financial requirements and methodological limitations in existing economic evaluations complicate conclusions regarding cost-effectiveness. Conclusions: The findings highlight the importance of procedure-specific evidence and balanced healthcare investment decisions. Robotic-assisted surgery should therefore be evaluated not solely as a technological innovation but as a healthcare intervention whose clinical value, affordability, and accessibility must be assessed together.

items.title: Rubric-Based AES with LLM Ensembles: Scoring of Student Responses in Critical Online Reasoning Using Ensembles of LLMs
items.abstract: Grading student responses is costly and time-consuming. Moreover, human annotators are prone to bias, fatigue, and rater drift, which further limits grading reliability. Various methods have been employed to develop automated essay scoring (AES) systems to reduce these costs and address bias-related issues. These methods range from early text-feature-based systems to current machine-learning and transformer-based models. Specifically, large language models (LLMs) offer the potential to streamline the development of AES systems. However, they are subject to well-known limitations, such as hallucinations and prompt sensitivity. This creates a need to explore the potential of a mixed-methods approach that leverages the synergies among individual LLMs through ensemble formation. We evaluate the potential of ensembles of LLMs to match human-rater agreement when grading student responses in economics and medical education across 103 criteria. We use 631 German-language responses and corresponding human ratings by 2 to 5 annotators from a previously conducted assessment. We experiment with 523 rubric-based prompt configurations across 15 open-weight LLMs and assess their consistency with human raters using Krippendorff's alpha for inter-annotator agreement (IAA) and the Alternative Annotator Test (alt-test). Our results show that replacing one human rater with the best-performing LLM--prompt configuration maintains or improves IAA for 91 of the 103 criteria and that LLMs pass the alt-test for 90 criteria. Our findings suggest that current state-of-the-art LLMs can support AES of German responses in economics and medical education, reducing human workload and enabling faster processing, while validation against human ratings remains necessary.

items.title: Safe Resemblance, Silent Propagation: Limits of Text-Similarity Guardrails for AI Agent Safety
items.abstract: When AI agents relay information to one another, an output can preserve an injected instruction's effect on downstream agents even after its wording changes, yet legitimate quotation and template reuse can produce high textual overlap with the source, so text-similarity guardrails that attempt to flag the former risk conflating these two cases. We test this distinction using DonkeyRail, a public classifier combining BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR features, deployed in a controlled three-agent email relay, defining a behavioral measure in which an output counts as functional (the injected procedure induces fresh computations in two subsequent agents) independent of the detector's score, alongside legitimate controls that explicitly authorize quotation and reuse. At its default threshold the classifier misses 8 of 19 functional outputs while flagging 70 of 192 legitimate replies, with every completed quotation and template-reuse reply triggering a false alert; calibrating for low false positives on one template set does not transfer, as the recalibrated threshold detects only one functional output and still produces 15 false alerts on new templates. We also identify an operating-point error in all 21 published classifier configurations, where ROC interpolation replaces direct threshold application, and show formally that high AUC against a surface-level text criterion provides no distribution-free guarantee of high AUC against the behavioral target, while the existing evaluation labels lack the joint observations needed to estimate the gap. An authorization analysis further shows that identical visible transcripts can require different safety decisions depending on the governing policy, a distinction no observation-only classifier can resolve. These results argue for behavioral and policy-grounded evaluation over text-similarity guardrails.

items.title: Safety-Preserving Medical LLM Fine-Tuning via Bilevel Data Selection
items.abstract: As general large language models (LLMs) are increasingly adapted for patient-facing medical applications, improving medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks remains a critical challenge. Large-scale medical instruction data are essential for acquiring domain knowledge through supervised fine-tuning (SFT), but unsafe responses can undermine existing safety alignment. To address this problem, we propose Scalable Bilevel Data Selection (S-BDS) for safety-preserving medical SFT. By controlling selection-weight concentration, S-BDS enables reliable sample ranking over large candidate pools and identifies training examples that improve medical capability while controlling patient-facing risks. We combine clinician-validated safe data and selected data with unscreened medical instruction data for SFT, and jointly evaluate medical capability and patient-facing safety on HealthBench and PatientSafetyBench, respectively. Experiments across Llama and Qwen models show that S-BDS achieves the highest safe rates among all compared methods, outperforming the strongest baselines by 4.64 and 3.00 percentage points, respectively, while maintaining competitive medical capability. Further experiments show that varying the safety-oriented weight during SFT controls the trade-off between medical capability and patient-facing safety.

items.title: Same Papers, Different Verdicts: Tracing Version Drift in LLM Peer Review
items.abstract: Venues and benchmarks read LLM review scores as measurements of a paper, while providers replace their models within months. We audit twenty frontier models from OpenAI, Google and Anthropic on ICLR 2027 submissions while they were under review, with tests registered before the decisions. Between an earlier and a later version of Claude Opus and of Gemini, the share of papers placed on the accept side falls by 52 and 53 percentage points on 183 and 60 randomly drawn submissions, and by 43 to 79 points in six further paired comparisons, with no paper moving up in any of them. Stating a 30% acceptance rate in the prompt leaves a gap of 79 points between the two Opus versions. When score-stripped critiques are swapped between versions, the later critiques alone lower the accept share by 35 points for Opus and 51 for Gemini; for Opus the drop is 35 points under a third-party scorer and 24 after a rewrite that keeps each technical point and removes evaluative wording. On 57 papers, the percentiles of Opus 4.6 and 5.5 correlate at 0.73 while their accept shares differ by 44 points. On 99 to 119 submissions, the self-estimated percentiles of three models correlate with two human reviewers more strongly than a third reviewer does (point estimates 0.17 to 0.21, 95% intervals between -0.04 and +0.42). All twenty models give a 2 or a 3 in 473 of their 475 reviews, against 60 of 72 human reviews. Retrospective tests on decided papers can draw on memory. Claude Opus 5.5 names the true first author of 27 decided ICLR 2026 papers from their titles alone, with no wrong name, and Claude Opus 4.6 accepted all 11 decided papers it said it recognized, against 5 expected. Thresholds on LLM-reviewer scores therefore have to be validated against human decisions for each model version; our tests against the ICLR 2027 decisions follow on 16 December 2026.
